title.en: Reactions of carbon compounds, ethanol, ethanoic acid and soaps

text.en: Gas stoves burn carbon compounds, vinegar is an acid and soap cleans oily dirt. All of them show chemical properties of carbon compounds.

Combustion: carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water, heat and light. Saturated compounds burn with a clean blue flame and unsaturated ones with a sooty yellow flame.
Oxidation: alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids using alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate.
Addition reaction: unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of nickel or palladium catalyst. This hydrogenation makes vegetable oils into fats.
Substitution reaction: in sunlight, saturated hydrocarbons like methane replace hydrogen with chlorine.
Ethanol is a liquid that dissolves in water. It reacts with sodium to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen. Drinking pure ethanol is harmful, so industrial alcohol is denatured.
Ethanoic acid, also called acetic acid, freezes at 17 degrees Celsius and is called glacial acetic acid. Vinegar is a 5 to 8 per cent solution.
Esterification: an alcohol and a carboxylic acid react in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form an ester with a sweet smell, plus water.
Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. Their molecules have a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail, forming micelles around grease. In hard water soaps form scum, so detergents are used.

problem.en: What happens when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate?

text.en: Carbon dioxide is released and effervescence is seen.

prompt.en: What are the main reactions of carbon compounds?

points.en: Combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution are key reactions.
Ethanol reacts with sodium; ethanoic acid reacts with carbonates and forms esters.
Soap micelles trap grease; detergents work in hard water.
